name: Hilbert's Problems
statement: A list of 23 problems posed in 1900 that set the agenda for 20th-century mathematics.
meaning: Hilbert's problems are a list of 23 problems in mathematics published by the German mathematician David Hilbert. He presented 10 of them at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris on 8 August 1900, in his address titled Mathematical Problems, and the full list of 23 appeared shortly afterward. Ranging across foundations, number theory, algebra, geometry, analysis, and the axiomatization of physics, the problems were extraordinarily influential and set much of the agenda for twentieth-century mathematics. Several became famous in their own right. The first problem is the continuum hypothesis, whether there is a cardinality strictly between that of the integers and that of the real numbers, which was later shown to be independent of the standard axioms of set theory, Godel proving its consistency and Cohen its independence. The second concerns the consistency of the axioms of arithmetic, a question bound up with Godel's incompleteness theorems. The eighth problem includes the Riemann hypothesis and Goldbach's conjecture, both still open. The tenth asks for an algorithm to decide whether a Diophantine equation has integer solutions, and was shown to be unsolvable, no such algorithm existing, by the MRDP theorem completed by Matiyasevich in 1970. As a group the problems have been enormously fruitful, most now resolved, some still open, a few considered too vague, and they helped define the modern discipline.
mechanism: Hilbert's list worked as a program by identifying, with authority and clarity, the questions he judged most important for the coming century, and by framing them so as to be pursued. In his 1900 address he stressed that the presence of good open problems is a sign of the vitality of a subject, and he chose problems that were deep, central, and likely to generate rich mathematics whether solved or not. The subsequent history bore this out. Work on the first problem, the continuum hypothesis, led to some of the deepest results in the foundations of mathematics: Kurt Godel showed in 1940 that the hypothesis is consistent with the standard Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms, and Paul Cohen showed in 1963, by inventing the method of forcing, that its negation is also consistent, so that the hypothesis is independent of those axioms and can be neither proved nor disproved from them. The second problem, on the consistency of arithmetic, connects directly to Godel's incompleteness theorems of 1931, which show that no sufficiently strong consistent system can prove its own consistency. The tenth problem, on Diophantine equations, was answered negatively by the combined work of Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam, Julia Robinson, and Yuri Matiyasevich, whose 1970 contribution completed the MRDP theorem showing that no algorithm can decide the solvability of all Diophantine equations. Other problems spurred whole subfields. Because the problems were so influential, tracking which are solved, partially resolved, still open, or ill-posed has itself been an ongoing project, and the tallies vary by interpretation.

examples.text: Hilbert's first problem was shown independent of set theory, Godel proving consistency in 1940 and Cohen independence in 1963.
The tenth problem, on deciding Diophantine equations, was shown unsolvable by the MRDP theorem completed by Matiyasevich in 1970.
The eighth problem includes the Riemann hypothesis and Goldbach's conjecture, both of which remain open.

whyItMatters: Hilbert's problems are among the most influential documents in the history of mathematics, shaping the direction of the entire twentieth century. By naming, at the very start of the century and with the authority of one of the age's greatest mathematicians, the 23 questions he thought most important, Hilbert gave the field a shared agenda and a set of grand challenges whose pursuit generated vast amounts of mathematics, launched whole subdisciplines, and produced some of the deepest results ever obtained, including the independence of the continuum hypothesis and the unsolvability of the tenth problem. The list embodied Hilbert's conviction that mathematics advances through the solving of well-posed problems, expressed in his optimism that every mathematical question can ultimately be answered, later voiced in his 1930 declaration that we must know, we will know, a conviction complicated by Godel's incompleteness theorems. The problems remain a touchstone, and they directly inspired the Clay Millennium Prize Problems of 2000, chosen a century later in conscious homage, with the Riemann hypothesis appearing on both lists.

working.text: identify the deepest and most central open problems of the field, as Hilbert did in 1900.
state each problem clearly enough to guide research and to be recognized when solved.
follow which problems are solved, open, or ill-posed as the field works on them over decades.

limits: Hilbert's problems, though enormously influential, are not a uniform or perfectly resolved set, and their status must be stated with care. Some problems are precise and have clean solutions, some remain open, notably the Riemann hypothesis within the eighth, some were shown to have negative or independence answers rather than the affirmative resolutions Hilbert may have hoped for, as with the tenth problem and the continuum hypothesis, and a few, such as the sixth on axiomatizing physics, are considered too vague or programmatic to count as definite problems. As a result, there is no single authoritative count of how many are solved versus open, and tallies genuinely differ depending on how one judges partial, disputed, or ill-posed cases, so any figure should be given as approximate. Hilbert's own optimism that every problem is solvable was itself qualified by Godel's incompleteness theorems and by independence results. The address was delivered on 8 August 1900 in Paris and presented 10 of the 23 problems, the we must know, we will know declaration comes from a separate 1930 Konigsberg address rather than the 1900 lecture, and the resolutions of the first and tenth problems are due to Godel and Cohen, and to the MRDP collaboration, respectively.
misreadings: Hilbert's problems are not all solved, since some, like the Riemann hypothesis, remain open, and not all were resolved affirmatively, since several had negative or independence answers. The list is not perfectly well-posed, since a few problems are too vague to count as definite. And the famous we must know, we will know is not from the 1900 problems address but from a later 1930 speech, so treating the problems as all solved, as all affirmative, or as the source of that quotation, misreads them.
origin: David Hilbert's list of 23 problems, 10 presented at the 1900 International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris, that set much of the agenda for twentieth-century mathematics and inspired the later Millennium Prize Problems.
